name: Jjimjilbang

card.summary: A Korean bathhouse and sauna complex where visitors soak, sweat and have their skin exfoliated with a scrub, used as a regular skin-care and relaxation ritual for smoother-looking skin.
card.aka: Korean bathhouse; Korean spa; jjimjilbang sauna
card.note: Hot rooms are not suited to everyone; hygiene standards vary by facility.

quick.overview:
A jjimjilbang is a large Korean bathhouse complex with gender-separated bathing areas, hot and cold pools and a range of themed sauna rooms, plus shared lounges where guests rest in provided clothing. Many visits include seshin, a vigorous full-body exfoliation scrub with a rough cloth.

For appearance, the draw is smoother, cleaner-looking skin from the scrub and soak, plus the relaxation and sleep-friendly environment. The only published research located on the practice is an uncontrolled Japanese study of charcoal-kiln sauna bathing, which found improved mood and anxiety scores.
quick.how: Visitors typically pay a single entry fee, shower, soak in the baths, then move between kiln and themed rooms in the provided uniform, resting and snacking between sessions. Optional scrubbing and massage are offered by attendants. Many people go weekly or monthly, and some facilities are open overnight.
quick.risks: Heat exposure is not suitable for everyone, and people with heart conditions, pregnancy or heat intolerance are generally advised by health bodies to be cautious with saunas. Hygiene of facilities, clothing and food has been questioned in Korea; hard scrubbing can irritate the skin.

lead: A jjimjilbang is a Korean bathhouse and sauna complex that became popular in South Korea in the 1990s. It combines gender-separated wet areas, with hot tubs, cold pools, showers and massage tables, with mixed-gender dry rooms including kiln saunas, salt and ice rooms, and lounge areas with heated floors where guests rest or sleep. [1][2]

People use it in looksmaxxing and skin-care contexts for the scrubbing and soaking ritual. The seshin exfoliation removes loose surface skin, and a soak followed by sauna time is described as a way to leave skin cleaner and smoother and to relax. [1]
Research on the facilities themselves is minimal. A 2008 uncontrolled study of 45 volunteers visiting a charcoal-kiln sauna in Japan reported improved mood and lower anxiety scores after bathing. [3]

chain: Soak and sweat in hot baths and sauna rooms
angle.text: The routine pairs warm soaking with manual exfoliation, so skin looks smoother and cleaner afterward. The sauna and lounge time adds relaxation, which people associate with looking rested.

paras: Entry typically involves gender-labelled doors, a shoe locker key exchanged for a clothes locker key, then showering. Guests wear provided shirts and shorts in the shared areas. Kiln rooms are often themed with jade, salt or minerals and range from roughly 15 to 50 degrees Celsius, with temperatures posted at the entrance. [2]

Facilities also include snack bars, heated floors for napping, televisions, exercise rooms and internet cafes. Some provide bunk beds or mats, and some men who live away from home or work late use them as overnight lodging. [2] Traditional snack items include steamed eggs and sikhye, a sweet rice drink. [1]

The kiln sauna, hanjeungmak, is first mentioned in the Annals of Sejong in the 15th century and was described as medicinal. Buddhist monks maintained state-supported saunas, and separate facilities for men and women have existed since 1429. [2]

Modern public bathhouses called mogyoktang spread in the 1950s and 1960s, and the combined jjimjilbang format with multiple saunas and leisure spaces emerged in the early 1990s. [1] Today hanjeungmak are usually part of a jjimjilbang rather than standalone sites. [2]

Seshin is a full-body exfoliation using a rough cloth, often performed by an attendant after soaking softens the skin. It removes dead surface skin cells. [1] No controlled study of scrub or bathhouse routines on skin appearance has been published.

A 2008 uncontrolled intervention study of 45 volunteers (mean age 51.9) at a bamboo charcoal kiln sauna in Japan measured mood and anxiety before and after bathing and found all mood scales and both anxiety measures improved; the authors listed the lack of a control group as a limitation. [3] No study found examines skin appearance outcomes of jjimjilbang use.

Wikipedia notes that the sanitation of facilities, clothing and food has been questioned, and that concerns about clothing worsening atopic skin or spreading parasites were raised without conclusive evidence. Health standards are set by South Korea's Public Health Control Act. Theft of smartphones is occasionally a problem. [2]

timeline.event: Separate state-supported sauna facilities for men and women begin, per the Annals of Sejong period. [2]
Public bathhouses (mogyoktang) proliferate in cities after the Korean War. [1]
The multi-sauna jjimjilbang complex becomes popular in South Korea. [1][2]
